# All-degree concavity of arithmetic power sums and concave-root tails

The parameter `d` in this note may be any real number `d>=1`.
Set `D=d+1` and `p=1/D`. No continuous concavity in the shift variable
is assumed. The result is a discrete concavity theorem and, subsequently,
a scalar closed-tail theorem. It does not prove an oblique mixed-integer
halfspace bound.

## 1. A convex power-increment function

For every real `x`, define

`g(x)=[(x+1)_+^D-x_+^D]^(1/d)`.

Then `g` is convex on the whole real line. Indeed,

`g(x)=D^(1/d) [integral_0^1 (x+s)_+^d ds]^(1/d)`.

The positive-part function is convex pointwise. For `0<=theta<=1`,

`((1-theta)x+theta y+s)_+
 <=(1-theta)(x+s)_+ + theta(y+s)_+`.

Monotonicity of the `L_d` norm on nonnegative functions, followed by
Minkowski's inequality, proves the convexity assertion. This includes
`d=1`. We will use both

`g(x+1)+g(x-1)>=2g(x)`                                 (1)

and, for `x>=0`,

`g(x-1)<=x^(D/d)`.                                    (2)

The latter follows by raising to the power `d` and dropping the
nonnegative term `(x-1)_+^D`.

## 2. The equality barrier and its exact sign characterization

Fix `q>1`. For `F>=q^d`, write

`E_q(F)=(F+(q+1)^d)^p+(F-q^d)^p-2F^p`.

There exists a unique `B(q)>q^d` such that `E_q(B(q))=0`, and

`E_q(F)<=0  if and only if  q^d<=F<=B(q)`.               (3)

Proof. Put `A=(q+1)^d`, `b=q^d`, and consider

`h(s)=(1+As)^p+(1-bs)^p-2`, `0<=s<=1/b`.

This function is strictly concave, `h(0)=0`, and
`h'(0)=p(A-b)>0`. At its other endpoint,

`h(1/b)=(1+A/b)^p-2<0`,

because `q>1` implies `A/b<2^d`, and `1+2^d<2^(d+1)`.
The strictly decreasing secant slope `h(s)/s`, for `s>0`, therefore
has exactly one zero `s_*` in `(0,1/b)`. It is positive before that
zero and negative after it. Since

`E_q(F)=F^p h(1/F)`,

take `B(q)=1/s_*` to obtain uniqueness and (3). This proves every
sign assertion used below; no extremum or root is left unattained.
QED.

## 3. The equality barriers dominate the next arithmetic increment

For every `q>1`,

`B(q+1)>=B(q)+(q+1)^d`.                               (4)

Proof. Let `U=B(q)^p`. By the equality defining `B(q)`, there is a
single `delta>0` such that the three neighboring roots are

`(B(q)-q^d)^p=U-delta`,
`B(q)^p=U`,
`(B(q)+(q+1)^d)^p=U+delta`.

The first quantity is positive, so `x:=U/delta>1`. Raising the
successive differences to the power `1/d` gives the exact identities

`q=delta^(D/d) g(x-1)`,
`q+1=delta^(D/d) g(x)`.

Convexity (1) yields

`delta^(D/d) g(x+1)>=2(q+1)-q=q+2`.

Equivalently,

`(U+2delta)^D-(U+delta)^D >= (q+2)^d`.                 (5)

Put `G=B(q)+(q+1)^d=(U+delta)^D`. By (5),

`(G+(q+2)^d)^p <= U+2delta`,
`(G-(q+1)^d)^p = U`.

It follows that `E_(q+1)(G)<=0`. Since `G>(q+1)^d`, the exact
sign characterization (3) gives `G<=B(q+1)`, proving (4). QED.

## 4. The first three partial sums

For every starting value `rho>0`, define

`A_m=sum_(j=0)^m (rho+j)^d`, `m=0,1,2,...`.

Then the first three roots satisfy

`A_2^p+A_0^p<=2 A_1^p`.                               (6)

Proof. Let `U_0=A_0^p=rho^(d/D)`, `U_1=A_1^p`,
`delta=U_1-U_0>0`, and `t=U_0/delta>0`. Directly,

`rho=delta^(D/d) t^(D/d)`,
`rho+1=delta^(D/d) g(t)`.

Equations (1)--(2) imply

`g(t+1)>=2g(t)-g(t-1)>=2g(t)-t^(D/d)`.

Multiply by `delta^(D/d)` to obtain

`delta^(D/d)g(t+1)>=2(rho+1)-rho=rho+2`.

Raising to the power `d` gives

`(U_1+delta)^D-U_1^D >= (rho+2)^d`.

The left endpoint `U_1^D` equals `A_1`; therefore
`A_2^p<=U_1+delta=2U_1-U_0`, which is (6). QED.

## 5. Arithmetic power-sum theorem in every degree

For every `rho>0` and `d>=1`, the sequence

`m -> [sum_(j=0)^m (rho+j)^d]^(1/(d+1))`, `m>=0`,

is concave at every integer midpoint `m>=1`.

Proof. At `m=1`, (6) proves concavity. Equivalently, by (3) with
`q=rho+1>1`, it says `A_1<=B(rho+1)`. Suppose inductively that
`A_m<=B(rho+m)` for some `m>=1`. Then (4) gives

`A_(m+1)=A_m+(rho+m+1)^d
 <=B(rho+m)+(rho+m+1)^d
 <=B(rho+m+1)`.

Thus the barrier bound holds at every `m>=1`. Applying (3) at that
`m`, and using the defining arithmetic increments of `A_m`, gives
`A_(m+1)^p+A_(m-1)^p<=2A_m^p`. QED.

In particular, for

`S_d(q)=sum_(j>=0)(q-j)_+^d`,

one has, for every `d>=1` and every `q>1`,

`S_d(q+1)^p+S_d(q-1)^p<=2S_d(q)^p`.                    (7)

For noninteger `q`, take its fractional part `rho in (0,1)` and write
`q=m+rho`, where `m>=1`. For integer `q>=2`, take `rho=1` and
`m=q-1>=1`; the possible zero endpoint term is zero since `d>=1`.
These choices identify all three sums in (7) with the consecutive
partial sums in the theorem. There is no undefined zero-to-zero power
and no approximation or interchange of infinite sums: the defining
sums have finite support for each `q`.

## 6. Tail concavity for every positive concave-root sequence

Let `a_l,...,a_r>0` and suppose `h_i=a_i^(1/d)` is a concave sequence,
with `d>=1`. Put `F_i=sum_(j=i)^r a_j`. Then

`i -> F_i^(1/(d+1))`, `i=l,...,r`,

is concave. The artificial terminal value `F_(r+1)=0` is not asserted
to be a concavity node.

Proof. Consider an interior index `i`, and write `F=F_i`,
`A=a_(i-1)`, `b=a_i`. If `A<=b`, then
`F_(i-1)+F_(i+1)=2F+A-b<=2F`; concavity of the power `p` proves the
required inequality.

If `A>b`, set `delta=A^(1/d)-b^(1/d)>0` and
`q=b^(1/d)/delta`. Concavity of `h` and positivity of `h_(i+1)`
imply `q>1`. Concavity also gives, for every available nonnegative `k`,

`a_(i+k)<=delta^d (q-k)_+^d`.

Extending the sequence by zero past its upper support for this estimate
only, one obtains

`b<=F<=F_max:=delta^d S_d(q)`.

Equation (7) says

`(F_max+A)^p+(F_max-b)^p<=2F_max^p`.

To transfer this inequality to `F`, use the concave function
`h(s)=(1+As)^p+(1-bs)^p-2`, with `h(0)=0`. Its secant slope from
zero is nonincreasing. Since `1/F>=1/F_max`, the inequality
`h(1/F_max)<=0` implies `h(1/F)<=0`. Multiplying by `F^p` proves

`(F+A)^p+(F-b)^p<=2F^p`,

the desired midpoint inequality. The endpoint cases require no
concavity comparison. QED.

## 7. Exact closed-tail bound at an integer mean

Normalize `sum_i a_i=1`, and suppose the mean
`m=sum_i i a_i` is an integer. Then both closed tails obey

`sum_(i>=m) a_i >= [(d+1)/(d+2)]^(d+1)`,
`sum_(i<=m) a_i >= [(d+1)/(d+2)]^(d+1)`.                (8)

Proof. A singleton support is immediate. Otherwise the mean lies
strictly between the two endpoints. Interpolate the concave sequence
`F_i^p` linearly on its actual index interval. Jensen's inequality gives

`F_m^p>=sum_i a_i F_i^p
 =sum_i (F_i-F_(i+1)) F_i^p
 >=integral_0^1 t^p dt=1/(p+1)=(d+1)/(d+2)`.

The second inequality is the upper-endpoint Riemann-sum inequality for
the increasing function `t^p`, on the finite tail-value partition.
Here `F_(r+1)=0` is used only as a partition endpoint, not as a
concavity node. Raising to the power `1/p` proves the upper-tail bound.
Reflecting the index sequence proves the lower-tail bound. QED.

The constant in (8) is sharp as an infimum even with exactly integer
means. To see this, use unnormalized masses `a_j(L)=(L-j)_+^d` at
nonnegative integers. For `L>1` their mean `m(L)` is continuous and
strictly increasing. Continuity includes integer values of `L`, since
a newly born mass has value zero. Strict increase follows from the
strict increase, for `j>i`, of
`[(L-j)/(L-i)]^d` on every fixed positive support interval; expanding
the difference of two weighted means as a sum over pairs proves the
monotone-likelihood-ratio implication. New upper support points
reinforce it. Moreover `m(L)->0` as `L` decreases to one, and Riemann
sums give

`m(L)/L -> 1/(d+2)` as `L->infinity`.

Thus for every positive integer `k` there is `L_k>1` with `m(L_k)=k`,
and `L_k->infinity`. A second Riemann-sum limit gives

`sum_(j>=k)(L_k-j)_+^d / sum_(j>=0)(L_k-j)_+^d
 -> integral_(1/(d+2))^1 (1-t)^d dt
       / integral_0^1 (1-t)^d dt
 =[(d+1)/(d+2)]^(d+1)`.

## 8. Mixed-geometric scope

For one integer coordinate and full-dimensional positive continuous
fibers of dimension `d`, their volumes have concave `d`th roots by
Brunn--Minkowski. Thus (8) applies to vertical closed caps at an
integer-valued marginal mean in every continuous dimension. It extends
the previously proved `d=1,2,3` scalar result without a loss in the
constant. It does not assert concavity of the scalar density obtained by
summing oblique projected fibers, and it does not prove (OC).
